Industry News: Fiona the hippo honored by US Senate in unanimous resolution praising Cincinnati Zoo staff

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fiona, the beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo, has died after swallowing a visitor's knit hat.
  • It has been revealed that fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U.
  • Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fiona, the beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo, has died after swallowing a visitor's knit hat.

It has been revealed that fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent.

Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT.

Industry observers note that fiona, a Nile Hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning three-years old this Friday, in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, Thursday, Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo).

Recent findings suggest that "The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno remarked. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart.".

The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was rolled out over the viewing windows into her habitat.

It has been revealed that "The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the zoo said in a Thursday statement. "Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.".

'WORST AQUARIUM EVER' REVIEW SENDS WHALING MUSEUM'S SALES SOARING 250%.

It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, walks into the Senate Reception Room in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, rose to international fame in January 2017 after she was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds. Her survival drew millions of followers online and inspired books, clothing, beer and an ice cream flavor.

Tributes poured in across Ohio and Capitol Hill following her death, with Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., praising Fiona on X as a "beloved presence" and the Cincinnati Bengals remembering her as "The queen of the Queen City.".

A representative for Moreno's office and the Cincinnati Zoo did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Fiona, a 9-year-old Nile hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday after ingesting a knitted hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. (Cincinnati Zoo).

#76965. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep.
  • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister right now serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he stated when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke mentioned.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” mentioned Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Matter One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” mentioned Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he mentioned, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with aims to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Sources indicate that zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services firm Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a firm registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

According to recent reports, SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which claims it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

According to recent reports, SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar.
  • Sources indicate that the 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure patch: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He noted the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for Upcoming Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the initiative for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost. #76963. Latest Update: The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1609 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
  • It has been revealed that democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
  • A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

It has been revealed that democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

In a recent development, but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the Latest Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

Passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or New Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

Moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

Sources indicate that legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

Industry observers note that we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

Our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

In a recent development, few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

We would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

It has been revealed that the 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

Sources indicate that if a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

On “The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets.
  • I think this fits a tech giant that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them.
  • JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets. That’s 12 more seats than JSX sells on its planes today, and it gives them a way to grow beyond the limits of their current operation. I think this fits a company that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me: JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX. New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for: Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft with 42 seats. Two aircraft initially, growing to six by the fifth month. 10,106 flights and roughly 309,000 passenger boardings in the first year. Flights averaging about 1.2 hours gate to gate, with staffing growing to 104 employees. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it confirmed an all-business class venture with beOnd. The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model. I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown. The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport. By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines. JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation. Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics. At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do proposal 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t stated what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration. Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the latest year, making the most of their coming majority.

According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

It has been revealed that arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, stated the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan stated.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she indicates of staffers headed there for the first time.

It has been revealed that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can swiftly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Recent findings suggest that some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

Sources indicate that there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, mentioned Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres remarked.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

It has been revealed that “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres noted.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

According to recent reports, those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, remarked he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the upcoming Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

According to recent reports, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren mentioned.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal stated he won’t be deterred by the letter.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” remarked Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

Sources indicate that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries remarked.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Sources indicate that beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet declared — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

Industry observers note that in prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin stated.

    #76958. Breaking: United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2275 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather.
    • It has been revealed that I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight strategy and the airline insisting on a weather diversion.
    • In a recent development, executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather. Three years later, they’re admitting it was all a lie. I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight plan and the airline insisting on a weather diversion. Now, Live and Let’s Fly flags the airline chairman’s admission that the passengers’ explanation was right. Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17. A dispatcher had entered the wrong destination in the paperwork. The pilots flew there. The flight attendants apparently believed they’d reached the city everyone bought tickets to. He described the weather explanation as “just a lie” and offered this advice: “The best way of public relations is to tell the truth, but tell it responsibly.” Passengers Were Welcomed To Abuja While Sitting In Asaba On November 26, 2023, flight 0504 left Lagos with passengers booked to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. It landed in Asaba instead, about 200 miles away. This was United Nigeria Airlines, not United Airlines. Passengers reported that the flight attendants welcomed everyone to Abuja but then everyone discovered where they actually were. November 26, 2023 — Peacock (@dawisu) Another passenger shared video: We legit got scared sha. Laff wan kee me 😅 pic.twitter.com/sWxbnJeDna— Lord Macky (@AugustineMacky) November 26, 2023 The airline’s original statement blamed “poor destination weather”, said the pilot knew about the diversion, and attributed the confusion to an incorrect cabin announcement. The plane eventually continued to Abuja. The Investigation Uncovered The Truth The flight used an Airbus A320 operated by Bulgaria’s Fly2Sky for United Nigeria Airlines. Fly2Sky said at the time that United Nigeria had assigned it a Lagos–Asaba flight the previous day and hadn’t requested a change during the pilots’ preflight briefing. The Nigerian regulator identified failures well beyond one person entering a destination incorrectly. In its findings there was: Poor coordination between United Nigeria’s operations center and the company supplying the aircraft. No joint preflight briefing between the pilots and flight attendants. United Nigeria’s failure to monitor the leased aircraft through its operations center. Failure to follow the approved flight plan filed with air traffic control. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it. British Airways Has Done It, Too In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with aims to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. Here’s the Instagram video from that coverage: View the video shared by @rizalhakimm_punyer on Instagram AirAsia X said it had intentionally diverted for fuel because bad weather had caused congestion at Incheon. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. Okonkwo also used his conference appearance to discuss a passenger upset that an advertised 11:30 a.m. flight had left at 11:20. He said he’d initially wanted to shout back, but instead responded, “I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.” An airline chairman giving a speech about accurately convey what on-time means.     Florida Passenger Barred By American Airlines—She Kicks Police, Spits In An Officer’s Face

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An American Airlines passenger was arrested in Florida on nine charges after being denied boarding.
    • Gianaras, 34, of Grayslake, Illinois, was arrested around 3 p.m.
    • Industry observers note that guessing Headlights reported the arrest and obtained the police and court records.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An American Airlines passenger was arrested in Florida on nine charges after being denied boarding. Police say she refused to leave the Tampa airport terminal, chest bumped one officer, kicked another in the chest, and spat in a third officer’s face. Ana L. Gianaras, 34, of Grayslake, Illinois, was arrested around 3 p.m. November 8 in Airside F according to the affidavit. Guessing Headlights reported the arrest and obtained the police and court records. The booking photo comes from the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office: Police say Gianaras yelled, cursing and screaming and that her speech was slurred and her breath smelled of alcohol. She was sitting at a bar when, according to the affidavit, she got off her barstool and struck one of the officer’s chest with her own. That’s when officers say they tried to arrest her. She tensed up and tried to pull away as they struggled to handcuff her. During a search, she allegedly kicked another officer in the chest with a “reverse single leg kick.” Then, as another officer attempted to place her in the rear seat of a patrol car, police say she turned and spat in his face. Police say they found: Five cannabis cigarettes. Two plastic tubes containing suspected THC oil. 6.9 grams of orange pills identified as 30 milligram Adderall tablets. The affidavit reports preliminary positive field tests for the cannabis and oil and that she couldn’t produce a prescription for the Adderall. And once she made it to jail, sheriff’s deputies used a Taser but it’s not clear why. Her charges break down as: Six felonies: three counts of battery on a law enforcement officer, one count of resisting an officer with violence, and two counts of controlled substance possession involving the Adderall and THC oil. Three misdemeanors: disorderly intoxication, resisting an officer without violence, and possession of less than 20 grams of cannabis. She was booked at 5:21 p.m. on November 8. At her first appearance the next day, the court set bonds totaling $26,150. After two nights in jail, she was released November 10 on bond. I’ve covered an American Airlines passenger at Dallas-Fort Worth who was denied boarding for apparent intoxication and then attacked three gate agents with her phone. And there was the Orlando passenger who fled on a motorized suitcase after being refused boarding and allegedly spat at an officer. If American’s employees saw the same signs of intoxication described by police, keeping Gianaras off the plane was the right call. Their side of the story though isn’t clear. I reached out to American Airlines, and they did not respond.     Per Politico, the incoming speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries, wishes to massively increase federal entitlements:.

    I’m sorry: What? What is Jeffries talking about? Have he and those praising him taken leave of their senses? The United States is $41 trillion in debt. The federal government is running annual deficits of $2 trillion. We paid more in interest last year than we spent on defense. Medicare is unsustainable as it is. Social Security is just six years away from mandatory benefit cuts. And the Democratic Party’s leader in the House wants to add a vast new spending program onto the pile. Do my eyes deceive me?

    Sources indicate that charles C. W. Cooke is a senior editor at National Review and the host of The Charles C. W. Cooke Podcast.

    #76955. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (700 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, california Rep.
    • Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.
    • According to recent reports, but California Rep.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, california Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    According to recent reports, but California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, stated House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

    It has been revealed that leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    Sources indicate that working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very problem that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she mentioned. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he stated.

    Sources indicate that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez remarked. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    Sources indicate that amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    In a recent development, BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto mentioned.

If you’re switching between Amex and Bilt, Bilt’s instructions say to select check or PayPal first, then the other points option. Start your purchase through the relevant Rakuten merchant link, check the rate, and save the offer terms and receipt. Don’t apply a coupon from somewhere else when the merchant terms exclude it.     #76952. United Airlines Is Now Worst For Checked Bags, Delta’s Cancellations Nearly Doubled—What The Latest Federal Data Indicates

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 34m • 📚 Deep Dive (6771 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    United Airlines Is Now Worst For Checked Bags, Delta’s Cancellations Nearly Doubled—What The Latest Federal Data Indicates

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 34 min read (6771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~34 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines is now worse than American at handling checked bags.
    • The latest federal airline statistics show some results that don’t fit the usual reputations.
    • According to recent reports, the Department of Transportation’s November Air Travel Consumer Report covers September and the first nine months of 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines is now worse than American at handling checked bags. Delta’s cancellation rate has nearly doubled. And American, which has spent years bumping more passengers than any other airline, cut involuntary denied boardings 84% in the third quarter. The latest federal airline statistics show some results that don’t fit the usual reputations. It also shows why calling an airline “premium” requires more than nicer seats and better wifi. Strong operational performance isn’t enough but it’s the table stakes. An airline needs to get the basics right first, including delivering bags alongside their owners, as close to on-time as possible. The Department of Transportation’s November Air Travel Consumer Report covers September and the first nine months of 2026. Here’s the domestic flight performance through September, and I take a look at how this performance compares to earlier trends. Airline   On time2025   On time2026   Canceled2025   Canceled2026 Alaska Airlines*   77.44%   78.64%   1.01%   1.30% Delta Air Lines   79.57%   78.31%   1.19%   2.25% United Airlines   76.77%   76.20%   1.34%   1.75% American Airlines   73.09%   73.30%   2.57%   2.99% Southwest Airlines   78.10%   73.08%   0.85%   0.96% Allegiant Air   74.69%   72.59%   0.44%   0.73% Frontier Airlines   69.96%   70.21%   1.78%   2.15% JetBlue Airways   73.42%   67.74%   1.43%   4.08% Every airline listed canceled a larger share of flights than a year earlier. American ranks fourth for punctuality with an improvement of just 0.21 percentage points. Southwest and JetBlue each lost more than five points. United’s Premium Pitch Gets Ahead Of Its Operation United has improved its cabins, technology and network. I’ve argued that its broader schedule explains a lot of the customer preference Scott Kirby attributes to the brand. It’s a better airline than it used to be. Its operational results still don’t support treating it as anything close to an all-around leader. United blames the locations of its hubs, and states that it does well considering where it opreates. Its annual report points to hubs at the “most congested and constrained airports in the country.” It also benchmarks departures against competitors at its own hubs, rather than treating all airports as equally easy places to operate. In September, the category covering air traffic control, airport operations, traffic volume and ordinary weather accounted for delays on 8.57% of United’s flights, versus 5.78% at Delta. United also canceled a smaller percentage of flights than Delta or American through September, and it ranks third for on-time arrivals. But its punctuality declined and its cancellation rate rose from 1.34% to 1.75%. That’s nearly a 1/3 increase. And the weaknesses extend beyond on-time performance and completion factor. United ranks last for mishandled baggage. American was worst in full-year 2024, while United finished last in 2025. United remains last for the first nine months of 2026, and finished last separately in July, August and September. Here are mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags, with a lower number being better. This includes delayed, damaged, lost and stolen bags. Airline network   Jan.–Sept. 2025   Jan.–Sept. 2026 Allegiant Air   0.9   1.3 Southwest Airlines   3.9   3.2 JetBlue Airways   3.1   3.4 Delta Air Lines   4.2   3.6 Alaska Airlines*   5.1   5.0 Frontier Airlines   3.8   5.2 American Airlines   6.8   6.6 United Airlines   7.4   6.9 United mishandles bags at nearly twice Delta’s rate. American remains last if you look only at the mainline airline: 7.2 per 1,000, versus United’s 6.6. United Express drags down United’s network result, while American Eagle improves American’s. Missed connections can cause bags to miss flights, too. So baggage problems aren’t entirely independent of congested hubs and delayed aircraft. Passengers buying connecting travel, though, have choices on which airline to connect and United doesn’t get a pass there because its hubs are less reliable. Then there are wheelchairs. United and Delta handled almost identical volumes: 105,534 at United and 105,559 at Delta. United mishandled 1,269. Delta mishandled 373. Delta Warned That Its Problems Would Last Through Summer. They Did. Back in May, I covered Delta’s cancellation problems and its executives’ warning that fixing them would take through the summer. Pilot availability, crew scheduling and recovery after disruptions were central problems. Chief Operating Officer Dan Janki mentioned, “It’ll take us a little bit of time here as we work through it through the summer.” And Delta’s pilots didn’t actually go along with changes to contractual provisions that would boost reliability. They want something in return, and Delta hasn’t been willing to pay. Delta’s cancellation rate rose about 89%, from 1.19% to 2.25%. Subtracting the first-half figures from the latest report gives a third-quarter cancellation rate of 2.08%, versus 1.13% a year earlier. This is still a problem. Southwest’s Boarding Changes Had Costs That Were Easy To See Coming I warned before Southwest introduced checked bag fees that pushing luggage into the cabin would slow boarding and create more gate checking. Assigned seating then removed the incentive to board swiftly to grab the best available seat, while making passengers hunt for bin space near a particular row. By March, flight attendants were pushing back over the consequences. Southwest was trying to get more flying out of its aircraft while making boarding less efficient. Through September, Southwest’s on-time arrival rate fell from 78.10% to 73.08%. Southwest handled 71.1 million checked bags, down from 84.7 million, while scheduling almost exactly the same number of domestic flights. That’s 16% fewer checked bag enplanements, now that they charge most passengers separately. People are now carrying their bags into the cabin instead of checking them as often. JetBlue’s Nice Onboard Product Can’t Make Up For Their Operation I’ve long described JetBlue as good in the air and a mess on the ground. Mint can be excellent. Even coach offers has been relatively pleasant, although JetBlue is enshittifying it in order to make room for domestic first class seating. But the operation lets down the product. The first nine months were bad: 67.74% on time and 4.08% canceled, both worst in the industry and their cancellation rate was nearly three times the same period last year. The summer was worse. Combining the July, August and September figures, only 61.85% of scheduled flights arrived on time during the third quarter. JetBlue canceled 6.28%, about one in sixteen flights. In July alone, it canceled nearly one in ten. September improved substantially, to 71.98% on time and 2.13% canceled. JetBlue still finished last on both measures that month. Actually getting a handle on this won’t fix JetBlue’s finances. They’re a baseline for a turnaround. Disruptions add expense, make repeat business harder to win, and undermine the value of the product the airline is spending money to improve. JetBlue needs customers to be able to buy its flight without budgeting for everything going wrong. Alaska Has Been A Perennial Leader Alaska leads the network on-time rankings at 78.64% and canceled 1.30% of its flights. That’s a better cancellation rate than any of the three largest network airlines. This is a longstanding strength. Back in 2015, I was asking why Alaska didn’t get more recognition for running such a strong operation when Delta received so much of the credit. Buying Hawaiian added an operation benefiting from the islands’ generally favorable weather. I pointed out that statistical advantage last year, and Hawaiian is now included in Alaska’s figures. But Alaska’s ability to run a good airline wasn’t something it bought with Honolulu. It was doing that long before the acquisition. American’s Bumping Numbers Are Finally Changing American involuntarily bumped 684 passengers in the third quarter, down from 4,318. That’s an 84% reduction, with almost unchanged passenger volume. Mainline American’s count fell nearly 90%, from 2,042 to 208. I broke the news of American’s new mandate against involuntary bumping. Airport managers can approve more compensation to find volunteers. Employees are supposed to keep the door open and take a delay if necessary. Volunteers can even be confirmed onto the very next departure when it’s already full. That directive took effect September 30. Nearly the entire quarter measured here came before it. The 84% decline shows the improvement that was already underway as American became more willing to pay volunteers. There’s another American improvement buried in the network totals. Comparing the third quarter with the same period last year: Mainline cancellation rate: improved from 2.21% to 1.46%. Regional partner cancellation rate: worsened from 2.44% to 3.17%. Combined network: almost unchanged, from 2.33% to 2.34%. American’s own flights became materially less likely to cancel over the summer, while American Eagle erased that improvement in the combined result. The bumping change also leaves Frontier looking particularly bad. It accounted for 69% of all involuntary bumps in the third-quarter table, despite carrying about 4% of the passengers. Delta secured 49,231 volunteers that quarter and involuntarily bumped nobody. Frontier recorded 841 volunteers and 2,514 involuntary bumps or roughly three unwilling passengers for every volunteer.     The latest federal airline statistics show some results that don’t fit the usual reputations. It also shows why calling an airline “premium” requires more than nicer seats and better wifi. Strong operational performance isn’t enough but it’s the table stakes. An airline needs to get the basics right first, including delivering bags alongside their owners, as close to on-time as possible.

    I’ve long described JetBlue as good in the air and a mess on the ground. Mint can be excellent. Even coach offers has been relatively pleasant, although JetBlue is enshittifying it in order to make room for domestic first class seating. But the operation lets down the product.

    The first nine months were bad: 67.74% on time and 4.08% canceled, both worst in the industry and their cancellation rate was nearly three times the same period last year.

    Sources indicate that the summer was worse. Combining the July, August and September figures, only 61.85% of scheduled flights arrived on time during the third quarter. JetBlue canceled 6.28%, about one in sixteen flights. In July alone, it canceled nearly one in ten.

    September improved substantially, to 71.98% on time and 2.13% canceled. JetBlue still finished last on both measures that month. Actually getting a handle on this won’t fix JetBlue’s finances. They’re a baseline for a turnaround. Disruptions add expense, make repeat business harder to win, and undermine the value of the product the airline is spending money to improve. JetBlue needs customers to be able to buy its flight without budgeting for everything going wrong.

    Alaska leads the network on-time rankings at 78.64% and canceled 1.30% of its flights. That’s a better cancellation rate than any of the three largest network airlines. This is a longstanding strength. Back in 2015, I was asking why Alaska didn’t get more recognition for running such a strong operation when Delta received so much of the credit. Buying Hawaiian added an operation benefiting from the islands’ generally favorable weather. I pointed out that statistical advantage last year, and Hawaiian is now included in Alaska’s figures. But Alaska’s ability to run a good airline wasn’t something it bought with Honolulu. It was doing that long before the acquisition. American’s Bumping Numbers Are Finally Changing American involuntarily bumped 684 passengers in the third quarter, down from 4,318. That’s an 84% reduction, with almost unchanged passenger volume. Mainline American’s count fell nearly 90%, from 2,042 to 208. I broke the news of American’s new mandate against involuntary bumping. Airport managers can approve more compensation to find volunteers. Employees are supposed to keep the door open and take a delay if necessary. Volunteers can even be confirmed onto the very next departure when it’s already full. That directive took effect September 30. Nearly the entire quarter measured here came before it. The 84% decline highlights the improvement that was already underway as American became more willing to pay volunteers. There’s another American improvement buried in the network totals. Comparing the third quarter with the same period last year: Mainline cancellation rate: improved from 2.21% to 1.46%. Regional partner cancellation rate: worsened from 2.44% to 3.17%.     In a recent development, the catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term. As I wrote before the election, many aspects of this administration are clearly good from the conservative perspective, not just by comparison to the Biden administration, but to Trump’s own first term and previous Republican administrations since the days of Ronald Reagan.

    Industry observers note that you ask for the check, select the restaurant in the app, enter the check number and pay with your phone. Tips go to your linked credit card. You don’t need to have booked your table through inKind.

    According to recent reports, the business behind it is restaurant financing: inKind buys future food and beverage credit, then sells or awards it to diners. Restaurants get money now and customers later.

    Recent findings suggest that danny the Deal Guru flags the upcoming sale, and Costco’s Thanksgiving ad details: Pay $64.99 for $100 in inKind credit. The credit covers food, beverages and applicable taxes at participating restaurants. Costco lists the item as nonrefundable, and says the redemption code normally arrives by email within 24 hours. A 50% Purchase Bonus Works Out To 33⅓% Off Doctor of Credit reports a new 50% bonus on purchases of inKind Cash. Some customers are seeing $150 in credit for $100. For the same $300 in dining credit, that’s $200 through a 50% bonus offer versus $194.97 at Costco. The $5.03 difference is small enough that different credit card earnings could change which purchase is better. The amount you pay for inKind Cash doesn’t expire. The promotional portion has a three year expiration. Neither purchase earns another round of inKind rewards when you spend the prepaid balance. These Three Coupon Pages Are Still Live The current claim pages show these offers, each valid for 30 days after claiming: Claim offer   Minimum qualifying meal   Savings at the minimum $50 off $100+   $100   50% $25 off $50+   $50   50% $25 off $75+   $75   33⅓% Those percentages exclude tax and tip. New members can still get $25 off a first qualifying $50 meal through my referral link. I receive referral credit when you qualify. Use A Coupon Or Prepaid Credit On A Meal As I noted in October, the old stacking advice no longer works. You can’t take $50 off a $100 bill and then pay the remaining $50 with discounted Costco credit. The live coupon pages expressly prohibit combining the offers with an inKind balance or another offer. You can still earn inKind rewards on the eligible amount charged to your credit card after a coupon. At a restaurant showing a 20% earn rate, a $100 qualifying food and beverage bill with a $50 coupon leaves $50 to charge, generating $10 toward another meal. Tax and tip are additional.     Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa vows to rescind Abbott's H-1B visa restrictions despite admitting program abuse

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Greg Abbott discusses H-1B visas and immigration to his state on 'The Will Cain Show.'.
    • According to recent reports, texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) remarked she looks to rescind Gov.
    • In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Texas Gov. Greg Abbott discusses H-1B visas and immigration to his state on 'The Will Cain Show.'.

    According to recent reports, texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) remarked she looks to rescind Gov. Greg Abbott’s hiring freeze on H-1B visa workers at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even as she acknowledged that the federal visa program has been abused.

    In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.

    "Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa mentioned.

    Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing latest H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

    OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY.

    It has been revealed that governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaks at a press conference Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at The University of Texas at Austin. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images).

    "In the most egregious schemes, employers have even fired American workers and replaced them with H-1B employees, often at lower wages," Abbott wrote in his January directive.

    While Hinojosa vowed to scrap the restrictions, she conceded that companies have exploited the visa system.

    Industry observers note that "There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune. "Companies should not be getting a bunch of tax breaks for jobs to only then use that money to hire H-1B employees. That’s wrong. That’s happening right now. I don’t support that.".

    Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative from Austin, defeated Abbott in the Nov. 3 election to deny the three-term Republican incumbent a fourth term, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. With Republicans still holding a majority in the Texas Senate, rescinding Abbott’s executive orders offers Hinojosa an immediate way to reshape state policy without legislative approval.

    HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT FUELS 11TH-HOUR POWER STRUGGLE AS UPCOMING ALLIES RALLY TO REIN IN INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR.

    Texas Gov. Greg Abbott immediately halted latest H-1B visas. (Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that hinojosa also defended local school districts’ use of H-1B visas to recruit foreign educators, arguing that Texas schools struggle to find domestic teachers. Abbott’s directive, however, applies only to state agencies and public institutions of higher education, not local K-12 school districts.

    A representative for Hinojosa did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
