    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries noted, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    Recent findings suggest that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for prepares purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Industry observers note that democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    • Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S.

    It has been revealed that the British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

    It has been revealed that burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

    It has been revealed that daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

    On “The Complex Reputation of James Burnham”.

    In a recent development, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    According to recent reports, the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    Recent findings suggest that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an notable part of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” noted Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    According to recent reports, “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very manufacturer that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    Recent findings suggest that “We require age checks for chat, place consumers under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson mentioned. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    According to recent reports, myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She noted Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s upcoming arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    In a recent development, “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    Tech Report: Southwest Plans To End The Wait For Extending Its Schedules—11 Month Rolling Calendar Is Coming, Report Notes

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that southwest Airlines intends to stop making customers wait for batches of newly introduced flight dates and move to a rolling booking calendar roughly 11 months into the future, more like other airlines operate, according to a new report by Enilria.
    • I checked Southwest’s own booking calendar.
    • In a recent development, there’s some history here that helps explain what’s changing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that southwest Airlines intends to stop making customers wait for batches of newly introduced flight dates and move to a rolling booking calendar roughly 11 months into the future, more like other airlines operate, according to a new report by Enilria. That would make it easier to lock in a family vacation or flights to a cruise—and give its international partners more opportunities to sell trips that include Southwest connections. I checked Southwest’s own booking calendar. They’re accepting reservations through September 29, 2027. Their next extension is planned for December 17, when they’ll open flights through November 6, 2027. That’s 324 days into the future. That December release is still a batch. The plan to replace these releases with a rolling window isn’t something I’ve seen anywhere other than from Enilria. Southwest Has Already Sold Flights More Than 300 Days Ahead There’s some history here that helps explain what’s changing. On April 26, 2024, Southwest declared its first booking window exceeding 300 days. It was selling travel through March 5, 2025—313 days ahead. At the time, Southwest said its historical range had been 180 to 250 days, citing vacation planning, meetings and groups, Hawaii, and its international destinations as reasons to sell further out. With batch releases, though, the window shrinks every day until the next extension. You might be able to book ten months ahead on release day, then considerably less several weeks later. A rolling calendar keeps adding dates. The reported change would give customers roughly the same planning horizon whenever they shop, without needing to track Southwest’s next release announcement. Shorter Schedules Meant Fewer Reservations To Fix I wrote about Southwest’s tradeoff back in 2020: waiting to publish let the airline offer a firmer schedule, but cost them customers who wanted to commit earlier. An airline can decide where to put its planes before selling the seats, or sell a provisional schedule and fix customers’ reservations when its plans change. Southwest preferred to finish more of that work first. That gave them room to adjust for seasonal demand and aircraft availability without disrupting as many purchased trips. Their technology made changing flights expensive. In a 2010 investor presentation, then-CEO Gary Kelly explained that when Southwest canceled a flight: we have to manually rebook every single customer on that flight Southwest completed its move to Amadeus Altéa in May 2017. This allowed for automated rebooking during disruptions, better connection planning, and more sophisticated inventory management. So the technology that makes a longer selling window practical has been there for years. The commercial case for using it has grown. International Partners Have A Reason To Want More Dates Southwest increasingly needs to appear wherever customers are shopping. I explained how the Expedia deal would change their incentives when it was announced in 2025. If a customer searches dates Southwest isn’t selling, competitors get the business before Southwest even enters the comparison.     #76939. The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (878 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that hang on at the start of David O.
    • It has been revealed that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football.
    • Industry observers note that madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

    It has been revealed that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

    Industry observers note that madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”.

    Russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

    Nicolas Cage (John Madden) in Madden.

    Chuck Zlotnick/Amazon MGM Studios.

    Industry observers note that the patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

    In a recent development, A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game company EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a upcoming generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis indicates to Madden.).

    Through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a latest world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

    More important, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

    Industry observers note that madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

    Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

    On “The American Genius of Madden”.

    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five latest air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, mentioned Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz noted the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization blueprint so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    According to recent reports, senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., stated the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not major on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    It has been revealed that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he mentioned. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    According to recent reports, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy mentioned, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Sources indicate that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy stated. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he mentioned that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    In a recent development, the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford stated Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    It has been revealed that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    According to recent reports, bedford mentioned he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    Industry observers note that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    In a recent development, that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    In a recent development, “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., remarked Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    In a recent development, “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, mentioned, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the fresh people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she remarked.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he mentioned. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    Industry observers note that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Sources indicate that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., mentioned Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    It has been revealed that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve stated many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    In a recent development, that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Recent findings suggest that kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he noted. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    Sources indicate that “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for upcoming leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    According to recent reports, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    According to recent reports, “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., mentioned, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #76929. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (767 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that former Alaska Rep.
    • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

    The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Industry observers note that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has mentioned she had no connection to the scheme.

    According to recent reports, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    According to recent reports, "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer noted in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    According to recent reports, the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    • Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

    Americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly. But that’s not what the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has done when it comes to personalized pricing.

    Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

    Vladlena Klymova is a policy analyst at the Taxpayers Protection Alliance.

    #76915. An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (962 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting.
    • That is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating.
    • Recent findings suggest that the fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “significant three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was mentioned in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a latest Yalta, was underway? If that was the proposal, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

    That is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

    Recent findings suggest that the fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “significant three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

    Recent findings suggest that as alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

    In a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

    It has been revealed that and all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

    According to recent reports, no details have been released so far of what was said in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

    Sources indicate that from left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

    Sources indicate that to return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

    Industry observers note that any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “An Overhyped Trilateral Summit”.

    What happens to Airbnb when personal AI agents can look at a listing and instantly check the price on the property’s own website, where Airbnb doesn’t collect a commission?

    Using the AI agent Instinct, Skift compared 16 Airbnb listings with rates on the properties’ own websites. The direct site was cheaper in 10 — by as much as 42% — and one was essentially a tie.

    When an account on X questioned whether Airbnb’s profits would suffer if AI agents could compare prices right before guests book, CEO Brian Chesky replied: “You presume we could never offer a price-match guarantee.”.

    The post wasn’t an announcement that Airbnb will match prices on short-term rentals like it recently started for hotels. But it signals that Airbnb could, and the test suggests it may eventually have to.

    Industry observers note that kentucky’s top auditor says her office has uncovered $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste across state government and accused Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, widely believed to have presidential aspirations, of brushing off the findings instead of helping fix them.

    "I wish I could say that I had more support and help from the governor's office in Kentucky, but I haven't really. And that's one of the reasons why I'm very public with our reports.     "I need the backlash that comes when you see money just being flushed down the toilet, when you see that you're losing money, especially in Medicaid. It's money that should go to people who are actually in need, and we're losing those dollars.".

    Over the past year, Ball’s office flagged $836 million in wasteful Medicaid spending that was primarily driven by multi-state concurrent enrollment, where Kentucky continued paying monthly managed care capitation fees for individuals simultaneously enrolled in Medicaid in up to eight other states.

    When it comes to potential Medicaid waste, fraud and abuse, Ball told Fox News Digital it is unlikely that money can be clawed back, heightening the importance of stopping it before it begins.

    According to recent reports, • In an unprecedented trilateral summit in China this week, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down with President Donald Trump. Ahead of the summit, Trump set no metrics for observers to judge its success. The summit cannot be said to have failed: It was not designed to achieve anything, and it didn’t. Of course, the president reportedly went into the diplomatic event of the year with some goals in mind. He reportedly sought commitments to nuclear disarmament from his Russian and Chinese counterparts, neither of whom had an incentive to agree to such limits. If Trump persuaded them to assist America’s efforts to isolate Iran economically, he has kept it a closely guarded secret. Putin sought to make the summit all about his war on Ukraine, but the Russian autocrat secured no meaningful promises on that front from Washington or Beijing. Only China, it seems, got what it wanted from the summit, which took place on its soil. The event allowed Xi to pretend to arbitrate the conflicts in which his great-power competitors are embroiled. The affair was not entirely unproductive, of course. It produced many joint statements of principle, which essentially state that all parties have agreed to keep talking.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Recent findings suggest that A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    It has been revealed that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The fresh office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., mentioned the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide stated.

    Industry observers note that the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Sources indicate that senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries remarked at a press conference following the election.

    It has been revealed that while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    In a recent development, “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get substantial things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    It has been revealed that “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these problems,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    In a recent development, “This is the beginning of a fresh bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    Industry observers note that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    Industry observers note that at his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    Sources indicate that “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    Sources indicate that “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Recent findings suggest that pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Sources indicate that the entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he remarked at his news conference.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Former NYPD Chief John Chell and former NYPD inspector Paul Mauro are accusing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's new disbanding of the Strategic Response Group as a move to please his base, with little real change to protest response being made.
    • New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposal to gut the city’s tactical police unit is not what is seems, two former high-ranking NYPD officials tell Fox News Digital.
    • They argue the stunt is a political sleight of hand in which specialized officers responsible for handling violent protests will be rebranded under a different name despite the socialist mayor's promise to disband it completely.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former NYPD Chief John Chell and former NYPD inspector Paul Mauro are accusing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's new disbanding of the Strategic Response Group as a move to please his base, with little real change to protest response being made.

    New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposal to gut the city’s tactical police unit is not what is seems, two former high-ranking NYPD officials tell Fox News Digital.

    They argue the stunt is a political sleight of hand in which specialized officers responsible for handling violent protests will be rebranded under a different name despite the socialist mayor's promise to disband it completely.

    Recent findings suggest that "The problem is … day-to-day Latest Yorkers don't understand all this gas lighting," former NYPD Chief John Chell told Fox News Digital. "And they feel the angst of it.

    "But at the end of all that, this is nothing more than smoke and mirrors.".

    EXCLUSIVE: RETIRED POLICE SERGEANT PROBLEMS WARNING OVER MAMDANI'S NYPD SHAKE-UP AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING PARADE.

    New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attends a news conference at NYPD headquarters in New York City on Jan. 6, 2026. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images).

    The move to dissolve the Strategic Response Group (SRG) and replace it with a "first-of-its-kind" civilian dialogue team fulfills one of Mamdani's campaign promises as noted in the first sentence of his news release on the move.

    Recent findings suggest that but Chell and retired NYPD Inspector Paul Mauro are questioning whether it's all a facade to please the mayor's left-wing base and is a restructuring rather than a disbandment. They say the unit will likely be rebuilt under a upcoming name to continue dealing with mass protests, major crimes and counterterrorism.

    "The con here is that the SRG is simply being rebranded into an unknown name right now," Chell said.

    Industry observers note that "First of all, Mamdani did add … that there will be uniformed police standing by to take more forceful enforcement if necessary," Mauro mentioned. "So, what really changed? Well, he changed the name of that unit, and he inserted this civilian unit between those uniformed cops and the protesters.".

    The newly proposed civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD) is meant to work as a buffer between protesters and the on-duty police who will remain present at large demonstrations.

    "Socialism and public safety do not go hand in hand," Chell insisted.

    Mamdani’s office did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on the criticism of his plan.

    NY COP CALLS FOR POLICE PROTECTIONS AFTER PROTESTER HE ARRESTED HIGHLIGHTED UP TO HIS HOUSE, HARASSED HIS FAMILY.

    NYPD officers arrest a demonstrator during an anti-ICE protest outside 26 Federal Plaza Building in Latest York City June 10, 2025. (Mostafa Bassim/Anadolu via Getty Images).

    Both former NYPD officials warned that relying on civilians to mediate rowdy crowds could delay police intervention if a peaceful protest turns into a violent riot. This, he stated, could leave officers responding to an escalating situation rather than preventing it in the first place.

    Sources indicate that "Once a cop, wherever they're assigned, becomes reactive versus proactive, public safety suffers," Chell stated. "And [when cops] become reactive, they tend to hold back, and that can get them hurt. And it can get civilians hurt.".

    "That is one of the risks inherent in this thing," Mauro added. "That you deploy the civilians, they're trying to talk … and by the time the civilians turn around and say, ‘Police, we need help,’ it may be too late.".

    SRG receives information from the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau to be kept aware of known or potentially dangerous demonstrations that will require specialized training to de-escalate.

    The SRG unit is trained to handle crowds that have turned violent, beginning with verbal de-escalation. The physical training teaches officers how to get a noncomplying individual into police vans. A common tactic used by the SRG is bicycle crowd management, whereby officers can line up their bikes to build a barricade in crowds, using those formations for crowd control.

    Recent findings suggest that "The purpose of the SRG was to make sure that you had highly trained officers who could diffuse, spin down, but then control if need be, protests that were getting out of hand," Mauro noted. "That's why they were only deployed in about 6% of the instances.".

    MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS.

    During a budget hearing earlier this year, it was noted the SRG did not often deal with peaceful protests and was mostly only deployed for protests that turned violent. In 2025, NYPD reportedly facilitated 4,255 protests and the SRG was available for roughly 6% of them.

    Critics of the SRG, including the ACLU's Latest York affiliate, say the unit is inherently violent due to its counterterrorism specialization that they claim "suppress protesters" and disregards "focus on First Amendment protections.".

    The training manual, reviewed by Fox News Digital, distinguishes between "peaceful/compliant" crowds and those deemed "violent/non-compliant." It also identifies three categories of protesters: "everyday citizen," "professional" and "anarchist.".

    The first identifier under the "everyday citizen" protester immediately acknowledges they are honoring their First Amendment right to organize.

    FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT.

    The NYPD's Special Response Group's cycling training manual identifies three categories of protesters: "everyday citizen," "professional" and "anarchist." (NYPD).

    Despite the dismantling of the SRG, Mamdani's blueprint would still likely require police officers be present at larger demonstrations. The latest civilian-led group, however, would be there to attempt to de-escalate the protesters if it should show signs of turning violent.

    Mamdani has not yet said when the civilian-led team will be established or take the streets. He also revealed the creation of the First Amendment Support Team (FAST), a 30-officer NYPD unit that will help de-escalate crowds while the CDDD is being developed.

    CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

    Chell, who has unveiled he will be running for mayor of Fresh York City in 2029 when Mamdani would likely be seeking a second term, noted he doubts the new team will take form until at least 2028, if ever.

    "What's scary about all this, the mentality of how the mayor and his staff and his socialist friends want to run this city," Chell said.

    "If they get everything they want, we're gonna be a Third World city, and I don't know if we can ever get it back.".

    It has been revealed that on the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most notable midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    Sources indicate that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    In a recent development, the last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the Newly introduced York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how massive a role early votes will play in the outcome.
