    #76802. The Luxury of Children

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3044 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The Luxury of Children

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania.
    • Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.
    • The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

    Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.

    The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

    The story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

    In a recent development, the inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

    Humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

    Fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

    Industry observers note that the United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

    Recent findings suggest that that trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

    Recent findings suggest that this dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

    It has been revealed that there is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

    Sources indicate that or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

    In a recent development, another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

    Sources indicate that in the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

    Recent findings suggest that modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

    And modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

    There are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

    Sources indicate that apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal shows up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

    Many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

    According to recent reports, richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

    Industry observers note that if the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.).

    In a recent development, the same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very rapidly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

    It has been revealed that the coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: Upcoming York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

    Something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

    According to recent reports, demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

    It has been revealed that but for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More key, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The new dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

    Industry observers note that short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

    In a recent development, in this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

    If governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.

    At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    In a recent development, “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Recent findings suggest that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” noted Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    Recent findings suggest that “I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Recent findings suggest that leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” stated California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    In a recent development, #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, debuted his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, confirmed he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    Industry observers note that they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” mentioned Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    It has been revealed that RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Upcoming leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    According to recent reports, remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Sources indicate that investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    In a recent development, tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, confirmed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    Sources indicate that the  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who indicates she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    Industry observers note that after Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    Recent findings suggest that the last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    #76800. Industry News: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3094 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foxnews ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Physicist and energy researcher Oliver Hemmers explains the engineering failures and economic challenges behind the collapse of Nevada’s billion-dollar Crescent Dunes solar plant.
    • Industry observers note that TONOPAH, Nev.
    • Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Physicist and energy researcher Oliver Hemmers explains the engineering failures and economic challenges behind the collapse of Nevada’s billion-dollar Crescent Dunes solar plant.

    Industry observers note that TONOPAH, Nev. — An Obama-era solar power plant once hailed as a "clean energy marvel" and backed by more than $1 billion in federal support has gone bankrupt for a second time and sold for just $7 million — with the estimated taxpayer tab potentially reaching $507.6 million.

    Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower. The plant was designed to generate solar electricity even after sunset, using an emerging technology that promised to revolutionize green energy in America.

    The Obama administration bet significant on the project, backing it with a $737 million federal loan guarantee and around $275 million in Treasury grant awards as part of its broader $90 billion push to combat climate change and stimulate the economy following the 2008 financial crisis.

    OBAMA-ERA 'CLEAN ENERGY' SOLAR POWER PLANT STILL USES FOSSIL FUELS – AND KILLS THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY.

    According to recent reports, the Crescent Dunes solar plant's central tower is shown unlit, left, and illuminated by reflected sunlight, right. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital (left); Getty Images (right).).

    But the promise never matched the performance.

    After operations began in late 2015, leaks and equipment failures repeatedly knocked the plant offline, production fell short and cheaper solar alternatives undercut its economics — driving the project into financial ruin and leaving taxpayers shouldering the cost.

    The financial collapse comes 15 years after Solyndra, another Obama-backed solar company, went bankrupt and left taxpayers in the red for $528 million — a sum Crescent Dunes' estimated taxpayer tab could nearly match.

    "The Crescent Dunes solar project is a microcosm of what is wrong with Democrat governance: the Green New Scam, hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars wasted, fraud, and a cover-up," Rep. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital.

    OBAMA-BACKED $2.2B GREEN ENERGY 'BOONDOGGLE' LEAVES TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK.

    President Barack Obama signs the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act as Vice President Joe Biden looks on in Denver, Colorado, on Feb. 17, 2009. The legislation helped finance the Obama administration's push into renewable energy, including the federal loan program that backed the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images).

    Crescent Dunes sits about 13 miles northwest of the old mining town of Tonopah, roughly halfway between Las Vegas and Reno.

    The isolated facility, which Fox News Digital toured, is surrounded by miles of barren desert, scrubland and distant mountain ranges.

    Across the 2,250-acre federal site, more than 10,000 giant mirrors surround a 640-foot tower — the centerpiece of a system designed to overcome one of solar power's biggest limitations: darkness.

    Unlike ordinary solar panels, which convert sunlight directly into electricity, Crescent Dunes focuses the sun's rays onto a receiver atop the tower, heating molten salt to roughly 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit. The salt stores that heat in a massive insulated tank, allowing it to produce steam that drives an electricity-generating turbine long after sunset.

    Sources indicate that that combination made it the first commercial-scale U.S. solar tower to use molten salt to both collect and store the sun's heat. DOE projected it would generate 482,000 megawatt-hours annually, with a maximum output of 110 megawatts — enough to supply more than 75,000 Nevada homes during peak periods.

    Sources indicate that the Crescent Dunes solar plant uses more than 10,000 mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that stores energy. The stored heat is used to produce steam, drive a turbine and generate electricity, including after sunset. (Fox News).

    Recent findings suggest that solarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

    American developer SolarReserve developed the project, while Spanish contractor Cobra, a subsidiary of construction giant ACS Group, built it.

    Both held ownership stakes in the organization that owned the plant, Tonopah Solar Energy.

    Spanish banking giant Banco Santander also held an ownership stake in Tonopah Solar Energy.

    According to recent reports, then-Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., championed the project. In 2016, he called it an "engineering and clean energy marvel" and predicted that "Nevada will benefit for decades.".

    The project reflected the Obama administration's push to expand clean energy by using taxpayer-backed financing to help bring promising but commercially risky technologies to market.

    But Crescent Dunes demonstrated how expensive those gambles could become when they failed.

    Crescent Dunes' problems emerged almost immediately.

    A major leak in its molten-salt storage tank occurred in October 2016 — less than a year after commercial operations began.

    During that shutdown, Treasury approved a cash-grant payment in March 2017 under the Obama-era stimulus program — funding that later became the subject of serious fraud allegations.

    It went back online in July 2017, but restarting the plant did not resolve its performance problems.

    Even in 2018, its best full year through 2025, Crescent Dunes generated just 41% of the annual electricity output projected by DOE, according to federal energy records.

    Then another tank failure halted generation in March 2019.

    Seven months later, the repeated breakdowns and poor performance eventually cost Crescent Dunes its sole electricity customer when NV Energy terminated its 25-year agreement.

    Without its long-term power contract, Crescent Dunes spiraled into financial trouble, culminating in its first bankruptcy in July 2020.

    It has been revealed that the 2020 restructuring handed ownership to ACS through its affiliate, Crescent Dunes Investment, with Cobra running the plant. The turnaround plan counted on extensive repairs restoring production to 400,000 megawatt-hours a year — more than twice its best annual output.

    The hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    Recent findings suggest that A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    The plant restarted in July 2021, only for further molten-salt-tank leaks in 2022 and 2023 to force additional shutdowns.

    Although the plant resumed selling electricity under shorter-term agreements, it continued to lose money and relied on financial support from affiliated companies, court records show.

    REGULATORS ALLOW OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT TO KILL THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY, INVESTIGATION FINDS.

    In a recent development, by January 2026, it was back in bankruptcy court. This time, the billion-dollar plant went on the auction block.

    Mississippi-based Sons of Liberty Construction, a company owned by three brothers, bought it for $7 million in July and are attempting to revive it.

    Industry observers note that the plant was generating electricity during Fox News Digital's visit, although they mentioned it remained well below its initial intended output. Their efforts to restore the troubled facility are examined in Part 3 of this series.

    A timeline of the Crescent Dunes solar plant shows major equipment failures in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2023, along with federal financing, Treasury grant approval, two bankruptcies and the project's eventual $7 million sale in July 2026. (Fox News).

    Behind that history of breakdowns and bankruptcies lies a dispute over what failed: the solar technology, the construction behind it, or a combination of both.

    Bill Gould, SolarReserve's co-founder and former chief technology officer, blamed the project's Spanish construction contractor, ACS Cobra.

    "It was a tragedy of mismanagement," Gould told Bloomberg in 2020, accusing the contractor of delaying necessary work and designing a defective molten-salt tank.

    Recent findings suggest that an unnamed engineer who said he had worked at Crescent Dunes since its early development offered a similar account, blaming the tank failures on design and welding problems. He told SolarPACES in 2023 that the plant's solar collection technology had experienced comparatively few problems.

    "It's just the old tech that's having these troubles," the engineer noted, referring to the conventional thermal-power equipment.

    The sheer size of the storage system posed a significant challenge, according to Oliver Hemmers, a physicist and energy researcher who formerly led the Harry Reid Center for Environmental Studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

    "Ultimately, the larger you make those tanks that hold the molten salt, the harder the material science challenges become," Hemmers told Fox News Digital.

    Hemmers mentioned temperature swings of hundreds of degrees can cause the metal to repeatedly expand and contract, eventually creating cracks and leaks. He had not reviewed the plant's engineering plans but questioned whether the developers had sufficiently tested the tank design.

    "You need to have alloys that can withstand that heat variation without moving much. Otherwise, when the walls move, the vessel breaks, cracks and leaks. So I'm not sure how much research they really put into the vessel design," he remarked.

    Hemmers noted that Crescent Dunes relied on a massive molten-salt storage tank, while other solar thermal facilities have used multiple smaller tanks to reduce the stresses caused by repeated heating and cooling.

    Court records show how efforts to prevent further failures came at a cost.

    Recent findings suggest that when the plant resumed operations in July 2023, operators lowered the hot-salt tank's temperature from its original design level of about 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit to about 850 degrees. They later raised it to as high as 900 degrees, but the lower temperatures still reduced electricity production and revenue.

    A 2015 Department of Energy promotional poster touts the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada, highlighting its $737 million federal loan guarantee and projected annual electricity generation of 482,000 megawatt-hours. The plant later suffered repeated equipment failures and two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (U.S. Department of Energy).

    The receiver atop the 640-foot solar tower at Crescent Dunes glows as mirrors concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada, in August 2026. The troubled plant was sold for $7 million following its second bankruptcy earlier that year. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    As Crescent Dunes struggled to meet its production targets, competing solar technology was getting cheaper.

    Falling prices for conventional solar panels, known as photovoltaic panels, including those manufactured in China, undercut the project.

    Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, offering a simpler and increasingly cheaper way to generate solar power.

    Crescent Dunes, by contrast, uses more than 10,000 computer-controlled mirrors, called heliostats, to focus sunlight onto a receiver atop its central tower. The heat warms molten salt, which is then used to produce steam that drives turbines to generate electricity.

    The mirrored faces of heliostats at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a receiver atop the plant's central tower, heating molten salt used to store thermal energy. (Michael Dorgan).

    Crescent Dunes, however, has one key advantage: Its molten-salt storage system allows it to generate electricity even after sunset, something conventional solar panels cannot do without additional storage.

    Those same economic pressures have battered California's Ivanpah solar plant, another Obama-era project Fox News Digital reported on that uses thousands of heliostats to concentrate sunlight. Unlike Crescent Dunes, Ivanpah cannot store the sun's heat to generate electricity after dark.

    Fox News Digital contacted ACS Group and its attorneys but received no response.

    The project was backed by more than $1 billion in federal loan guarantees and grants.

    It has been revealed that that included a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee. DOE said it resolved its financial interests in the project through the plant's first bankruptcy settlement in 2020 in an effort to maximize taxpayer recovery and estimated its loss on the loan at $232 million — a figure the department confirmed to Fox News Digital on background.

    The Trump administration's Department of Energy blasted the handling of taxpayer money behind the project.

    Recent findings suggest that "It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green Newly introduced Scam. Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project," DOE assistant press secretary Caroline Murzin told Fox News Digital in a written statement.

    The project also received a $275.6 million Treasury grant award, which, unlike the loan, was not intended to be repaid provided the project met the program's requirements.

    Combined, the Treasury grant awards and DOE's estimated loan loss would put the total federal cost at approximately $507.6 million, although Treasury has not confirmed the full grant was disbursed and DOE has not provided a final accounting of its loan losses.

    Fox News Digital has filed Freedom of Information Act requests with both the Energy and Treasury departments seeking a full accounting of the federal loans, grant payments and taxpayer losses associated with Crescent Dunes.

    Rows of computer-controlled heliostats surround the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The mirrors track the sun and direct concentrated sunlight toward the receiver atop the tower. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

    The Treasury grant also became the focus of a private investor-backed lawsuit alleging that companies involved in construction fraudulently secured the money. A judge dismissed the case at DOJ's request and the investors are appealing.

    The allegations and the fight over the dismissal are examined in Part 2.

    Reid, who died in 2021, had championed Crescent Dunes as a showcase for government and private industry working together to build "the next generation of clean energy technology.".

    Its financial collapse has sharpened the question behind that partnership: Should taxpayers bankroll commercially risky energy projects that private lenders are unwilling to fully finance?

    "The government shouldn't be picking winners and losers," Véronique de Rugy, an economist at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, told Fox News Digital.

    According to recent reports, "This is not the role of the government. The government is not good at actually picking projects that somehow the private sector is leaving on the sidewalk," she said.

    Former President Barack Obama, right, is pictured alongside the Crescent Dunes solar plant in Nevada, left. The Obama-era project received more than $1 billion in federal backing before going bankrupt twice and selling for $7 million in July 2026. The images are a composite. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images).

    Industry observers note that de Rugy argued that politicians take credit for publicly financed projects without facing the same consequences when they collapse. Unlike private investors, she mentioned, politicians don't personally bear the financial losses when their bets go wrong.

    "So then they can go and do a ribbon cutting ceremony when the plant opens, and then they're usually nowhere to be seen when the company goes under," she remarked.

    She also argued that many companies receiving government assistance would have succeeded without it, questioning why taxpayers should shoulder the risks of commercial investments.

    "These subsidies go to projects that end up failing, right, then taxpayers have to shoulder the bill," she said.

    Nick Loris, president of the Conservative Coalition for Climate Solutions (C3 Solutions), a conservative energy and environmental policy think tank, offered a different perspective, arguing that government financing can sometimes justify the risks of developing new technologies.

    Sources indicate that "I wouldn't call it a mistake. I think it took a risky bet on a potentially promising technology that aimed to solve one of the challenges with solar in its intermittency," Loris told Fox News Digital.

    He argued that federal financing can help promising technologies reach the market when private investors are reluctant to take the risk, and that failures such as Crescent Dunes should be weighed against successful projects and interest earnings across DOE's broader loan portfolio.

    According to recent reports, one example is California's Desert Sunlight, a 550-megawatt solar farm that uses panels instead of mirrors and molten salt. In a 2024 assessment, DOE noted the project helped prove the viability of large-scale solar and was meeting its loan obligations.

    Recent findings suggest that across the broader program, DOE reported in its fiscal 2027 budget justification that borrowers had paid nearly $5 billion in interest, compared with nearly $1 billion in default losses, through Sept. 30, 2025.

    But Hemmers questioned whether Crescent Dunes ever made economic sense, arguing that the billion-dollar investment was a risky gamble from the outset.

    "Right, we kind of say, okay, that was a boondoggle. It didn't work. And so now we move on, right, do something else," Hemmers stated.

    "I think so, yeah. I think from the get-go, it started off too expensive, and I think it was unfortunate, let's say for the developer, that they run into all these technical problems on top of it," he stated.

    "And as we can see from that project, it completely failed in the end.".

    Congo’s Escalating Ebola Crisis

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The highlights this week: Health leaders concern new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.
    • The highlights this week: Health leaders problem upcoming warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.
    • It has been revealed that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus shows no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

    The highlights this week: Health leaders concern new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

    The highlights this week: Health leaders problem upcoming warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

    It has been revealed that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus shows no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is exacerbated by an underfunded health system and armed conflict in eastern provinces, where global mining projects have led to increased disease transmission.

    In a recent development, the outbreak is “still serious, and is still not under control,” said Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. The death toll since the outbreak began in May has passed 5,500 people, with more than 11,000 people infected, according to Congolese government figures released last week.

    Sources indicate that infections are now spreading at double the rate as when the outbreak began, according to Kaseya. More than 80 percent of upcoming cases are emerging outside of known contact lists, and more than 65 percent of deaths have occurred outside of healthcare facilities, he added.

    Kaseya called the lack of coordination between Congo’s government and foreign donors “a collective failure,” urging donors to release $1.6 billion in pledged aid.

    International donors have disbursed more than $962 million to organizations that are implementing Congo’s Ebola response. But around $700 million of that sum was unaccounted for as of last month, according to Kaseya. The Africa CDC mentioned that it was too early to attribute this discrepancy to embezzlement, but an investigation is underway.

    In 2020, Congo’s former health minister was convicted of embezzling more than $400,000 from funds intended to fight Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak.

    Meanwhile, Congolese health workers—who have not been paid for months—have gone on strike. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned last week that ambulances had run out of fuel, staff were untrained, and that the Congolese government and United Nations agencies needed to “strengthen oversight and accountability.” MSF has called the outbreak “out of control.”.

    For Congo, dealing with the Ebola crisis requires tackling systemic problems beyond healthcare, including poverty, conflict, and inefficient governance. But Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi appears to be focused on cementing his grip on power. On Nov. 9, he signed a law that critics say could grant him a third term in office.

    According to recent reports, congo’s 2006 constitution allows a maximum of two presidential terms and explicitly prevents parliament from changing those rules under any circumstance. The upcoming law lowers the threshold for holding national referendums and permits constitutional overhauls through referendums “in case of absolute necessity.”.

    Recent findings suggest that tshisekedi became president in January 2019; his second term ends in 2028. He has mentioned that he is not seeking a third term but would serve one if given a mandate by voters. “I have not asked for a third term, but I tell you this: If the people want me to have a third term, I will accept,” Tshisekedi said in May.

    On Nov. 1, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a newly introduced rebel alliance led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, sent a letter to U.S. officials and the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo warning that any constitutional changes could derail peace negotiations. Kabila’s alliance includes the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23.

    In a recent development, the Trump administration negotiated a peace accord between Congo and Rwanda in December 2025 that seemed to prioritize securing U.S. access to Congo’s critical minerals over tackling domestic government reforms and bolstering a weak state. Expanded mining in Congo’s forests has increased human contact with animals that carry the Ebola virus, according to scientists.

    Nearly one year on, amid an Ebola outbreak and on the precipice of further conflict, Congo is paying the price for the institutional neglect enshrined in the deal.

    It has been revealed that wednesday, Nov. 18: An Egyptian court hears the retrial of Lina Attalah, the editor in chief of Mada Masr, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The U.N. has described the charges against Attalah as an assault on press freedom.

    The U.N. Security Council hears a briefing from the International Criminal Court on its work in Libya.

    Thursday, Nov. 19, to Saturday, Dec. 19: Dak’Art, the biennale of contemporary African art, returns to Dakar, Senegal.

    Recent findings suggest that wednesday, Nov. 25: The U.N. Security Council is due to renew its sanctions targeting al-Shabaab and other armed groups in Somalia.

    Amnesty report on South Sudan. A new report from Amnesty International accuses South Sudan’s government and U.N. peacekeepers of failing to act on advance warnings of a March massacre that killed more than 200 people. The report came ahead of an announcement that South Sudan would again delay general elections to February 2027.

    The elections were previously scheduled for Dec. 22. The South Sudanese government did not cite a reason for the move, but authorities have repeatedly pushed back elections since 2022 amid a power struggle between President Salva Kiir and his ousted former deputy, Riek Machar.

    According to recent reports, A 2018 power-sharing arrangement between Kiir and Machar  broke down last year after an attack on a military base in Upper Nile state by an armed group known as the White Army, which killed more than 250 soldiers. Kiir accused Machar and his party’s military wing of colluding with the White Army, which Machar denied.

    Machar is presently on trial for charges including treason.

    Recent findings suggest that cape Verde elections. Cape Verdean President José Maria Neves was reelected on Sunday, capturing more than 63 percent of the vote amid record low turnout, according to provisional results. Neves’s main challenger, former Justice Minister Joana Rosa—the country’s first woman presidential candidate—conceded on Monday.

    The lack of opportunities for young people in Cape Verde was a major election topic. Rosa pledged to address concerns facing young people, while Neves promised to organize a summit to address youth emigration. According to data released in July by Cape Verde’s statistics body, around 65 percent of people aged 15 to 35 said they intended to emigrate.

    Neves’s party has dominated Cape Verdean politics since it gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

    In a recent development, madagascar’s ties to Russia. U.S. Africa Command’s deputy commander, John Brennan, warned against Madagascar’s strengthening ties with Russia last week, saying that Moscow is importing the “Sahel model” to the island.

    In a recent development, “We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent,” Brennan noted in a media briefing. Since the country’s 2025 coup, Russia has supplied the military-backed government with weapons—amid repeated calls from young Madagascans for a return to democracy.

    Industry observers note that some Africans perceived Brennan’s comments as lecturing from the United States. “America is not talking to Russia as a partner. It is talking to Madagascar as a client,” Fortune Madondo wrote in Modern Ghana, suggesting that the United States might condition assistance to needy Madagascar on its allegiance.

    Recent findings suggest that the criticism underscored why it’s important that U.S. officials consider how their comments land in Africa. If not framed carefully, they could play into Russia’s narrative that the United States is acting like a colonial power.

    Sources indicate that ghana to boost local manufacturing. Ghana will invest $10 billion over four years in a domestically funded “newly introduced economy” program to boost local manufacturing and jobs. Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told parliament in his 2027 budget speech last Friday that the funds will increase refining capacity and reduce lower-value raw materials exports.

    In a recent development, around $1.5 billion of the package will be allocated to financing refining facilities for gold, manganese, bauxite, and lithium. The Ghanaian government noted it is relying on tax reforms already approved by parliament, better tax collection, and revenue from oil and minerals exports to finance the program.

    The winner of this year’s 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza, has been cleared of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, “The Blue Fighter,” after an October article in the Atlantic said that the AI detection software Pangram found the story was entirely AI-generated.

    Sources indicate that the Atlantic article sparked pushback from Africa’s literary community. Critics remarked AI detection tools are disproportionately weaponized against authors from marginalized backgrounds. Following a monthlong review, the Caine Prize’s board said that digital forensic evidence demonstrated the article was human-written and that Kundizeza’s $13,000 award stands.

    Nigeria’s surveillance state. An investigation by Ajibola Amzat for the Center for Collaborative Investigative Journalism found that Nigeria has spent billions of dollars of public funds on surveillance technology that is supposedly intended to fight insecurity—but is routinely used instead to monitor protesters, journalists, and government critics.

    “Constitutionally guaranteed dissent is being watched and increasingly hunted while the terrorists and bandits freely operating in several corners of Nigeria’s 36 states remain elusive,” Amzat wrote.

    Europe’s externalized borders. On Monday, five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands—revealed looks to send asylum-seekers who have exhausted all legal avenues to Rwanda.

    In a recent development, in 2024, the United Kingdom scrapped a similar deal due to legal challenges over the country’s human rights record. Since 2019, the European Union has also funded a scheme operated by the U.N. refugee agency that temporarily evacuates refugees from Libya to Rwanda.

    In light of this week’s news, we’re revisiting Sally Hayden’s 2020 Foreign Policy dispatch from Rwanda’s refugee centers. “At what point does the EU become responsible for refugees it has forced from its borders through externalization policies?” Hayden wrote at the time.

    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., noted earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    In a recent development, when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Industry observers note that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack mentioned that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    It has been revealed that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack remarked in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., noted everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he remarked at Thursday’s meeting.
